terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation (-iō): with an accusative, or ut and the subjunctive
evidence: Caes. BG 4.29.1: quī diēs maritimōs aestūs maximōs in Ōceanō efficere cōnsuēvit
terms.comment: What is caused goes in the accusative, or in an ut-clause (efficere ut, Cic. Lael. 59, Lewis & Short); with a second accusative it is “make”: fortūna eōs efficit caecōs (Cic. Lael. 54, Lewis & Short). Traupman (p. 288) also gives facere ut: quid fēcit ut abīret?, what caused him to leave?

evidence: Cic. Mur. 1: pācem, tranquillitātem, ōtium, concordiam (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of what a thing brings on someone, with the dative: illī molestiam adfert, it brings him trouble (Ter. Hec. 344).

terms.gloss: stir up, cause (laughter, pain, a war)
terms.comment: Of feelings and bodily states: rīsum, lacrimās, dolōrem movēre.

terms.grammar: phrase: causa with the genitive of what is caused, or cūr
evidence: Cic. Phil. 9.7: is quī causa mortis fuit (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: be the cause, be to blame
terms.grammar: phrase: with ut or quō and the subjunctive
evidence: Liv. 40.26.5: vim morbī in causā esse, quō sērius perficerētur
terms.comment: Rare, and not before Livy (Lewis & Short). The Ciceronian example Lewis & Short gives, Fam. 1.1.1 in causā haec sunt, means “in the case, things stand as follows”.

evidence: Plaut. Capt. 4.2.20: faciam, ut ejus diēī locīque meīque semper meminerit (Lewis & Short s.v. faciō)

phrases.latin: crēscunt animālia quaedam minūta, quae nōn possunt oculī cōnsequī, et per āera intus in corpus per ōs ac nārēs perveniunt atque efficiunt difficilīs morbōs
phrases.english: certain tiny creatures breed that the eye cannot follow; they get into the body through the air, by the mouth and nose, and cause serious illnesses

phrases.latin: nōs causa bellī, nōs volnerum ac caedium virīs ac parentibus sumus
phrases.english: it is we who are the cause of the war, we who cause our husbands’ and fathers’ wounds and deaths
going along with people makes friends; the truth makes enemies
